claim: Apprenticed at 12 to brother James (printer) under a 9-year indenture; broke it at 17 after repeated disputes, later calling it 'one of the first errata of my life.'
source_title: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (Harvard Classics ed., ed. Charles W. Eliot)
limitations: Part One, written at Twyford in 1771 about events of 1718-1723; composed retrospectively ~48-53 years after the events; posthumously published (1791 French, 1793 English). Founders Online (National Archives) was inaccessible (automated bot-check); read the Harvard Classics/Eliot text instead.

claim: Governor William Keith's promised letters of credit for London (1724) never existed; Franklin was stranded in London about eighteen months working as a printer.
source_title: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (Harvard Classics ed., ed. Charles W. Eliot)
limitations: Part One (1771), recounting events of 1724-1726. Single-source account (Franklin's own retrospective); no independent corroboration of Keith's intentions was sought.

claim: Founded the Junto, a 12-member mutual-improvement club (1727), with rules against dogmatic assertion and direct contradiction.
source_title: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (Harvard Classics ed., ed. Charles W. Eliot)
limitations: Part One (1771), recounting 1727. Membership and rules as Franklin himself later described them.

claim: Founded the Library Company of Philadelphia (1731), a subscription library grown out of the Junto's pooled books; Franklin calls it 'the mother of all the North American subscription libraries.'
source_title: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (Harvard Classics ed., ed. Charles W. Eliot)
limitations: Part One (1771), recounting 1731; the claim of being the first/model library is Franklin's own characterization, not independently checked against a library-history source.

claim: The thirteen-virtue self-examination scheme (1730s): a tracking book with daily marks per virtue; Franklin reports failing hardest at Order ('I found myself incorrigible with respect to Order') while judging the project worthwhile overall.
source_title: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (Harvard Classics ed., ed. Charles W. Eliot)
limitations: Part Two, written at Passy in 1784, recounting the 1730s. Includes the Quaker friend's charge of being 'overbearing, and rather insolent,' which prompted adding Humility as the 13th virtue.

claim: Declined a patent on the Franklin (Pennsylvania) stove (c.1742-44) 'as we enjoy great advantages from the inventions of others'; an English ironmonger later patented and profited from a modified copy, which Franklin never contested.
source_title: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (Harvard Classics ed., ed. Charles W. Eliot)
limitations: Part Three, composed at Philadelphia starting August 1788 (per the editorial break noted in the Pine edition, Gutenberg #20203), recounting c.1742-1744. Only the Eliot/Harvard Classics text (Gutenberg #148) was read closely for the exact wording; part-boundary dating cross-checked against the Pine edition.

claim: From 1733, set up journeymen printers in other colonies as one-third partners on written articles; in 1748 sold half his own Philadelphia printing house to foreman David Hall on the same model, an 18-year partnership that funded his withdrawal from daily printing in his early forties.
source_title: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (Harvard Classics ed., ed. Charles W. Eliot)
limitations: Part Three (composed from August 1788), recounting 1733-1748+. The Autobiography does not give Hall's start date as a single explicit day; '1748' and 'eighteen years' are as stated in the text.

claim: 'Advice to a Young Tradesman' (1748): time and credit both treated as compounding capital ('Remember that time is money'; 'Remember that credit is money'); punctuality as a credit-building asset.
source_title: Advice to a Young Tradesman, Written by an Old One (reprinted in The Life of Benjamin Franklin, by Samuel G. Goodrich)
limitations: Read in full via a biographical reprint (Goodrich, Gutenberg #38469); cross-checked word-for-word against an independent transcription (biblioteca.scriptorium.ro, Complete Works vol. III). Founders Online (National Archives), which dates the piece 21 July 1748 and notes later reprints vary slightly, was inaccessible (bot-check).

claim: Letter to Joseph Priestley, 19 Sept 1772: the 'Moral or Prudential Algebra' — list reasons pro and con on paper, cancel roughly equal ones over several days, decide from what is left.
source_title: Benjamin Franklin, Representative Selections (ed. Frederick Lewis Pattee / Chester E. Jorgenson)
limitations: Read in full in the Gutenberg anthology (#35508); cross-checked word-for-word against an independent transcription (ahoona.com, citing Labaree & Bell, eds., Mr. Franklin: A Selection from His Personal Letters, Yale UP, 1956). Founders Online (National Archives) was inaccessible (bot-check).

claim: Letter to Joseph Priestley, 8 Feb 1780: regrets 'being born so soon' to see where science will lead; predicts human power over matter will grow enormously 'in a thousand years' (curing disease, extending life), adding 'O that moral Science were in as fair a way of Improvement.'
source_title: Benjamin Franklin, Representative Selections (ed. Frederick Lewis Pattee / Chester E. Jorgenson)
limitations: Read in full in the Gutenberg anthology (#35508). Founders Online (National Archives) was inaccessible (bot-check); its editorial summary of the same letter (from search-result snippets only, not a full read) is consistent with this text.

claim: Letter to M. Dubourg, 'Observations on the Prevailing Doctrines of Life and Death' (c.1773): flies revived after being drowned in Madeira wine; wishes he could be embalmed and revived in a century to see America's progress, preferring that to 'any ordinary death.'
source_title: Memoirs of Benjamin Franklin; Written by Himself, Vol. II
limitations: This English-language reprint gives no exact day for the letter (other finding aids suggest spring 1773; Founders Online, inaccessible due to a bot-check, lists several Franklin-Dubourg exchanges from that period). The text read is a 19th-century English edition, not a side-by-side check against Franklin's French original.

claim: Letter to Jan Ingenhousz, 16 Jan 1784: cheap balloons ('five thousand balloons, capable of raising two men each') could make it impossible to defend a border against 'ten thousand men descending from the clouds,' possibly 'convincing sovereigns of the folly of wars.'
source_title: Scientific Letters of Benjamin Franklin (ed. I. Bernard Cohen), reprinted in the Internet History Sourcebooks Project
limitations: Read in full via the Fordham sourcebook reprint of Cohen's 1931 scholarly edition (University of Pennsylvania Press). Founders Online (National Archives) was inaccessible (bot-check); its search-result snippet of the same letter is consistent with this text.

claim: Speech in the Constitutional Convention at the conclusion of its deliberations, 17 Sept 1787: 'I agree to this Constitution, with all its faults'; predicts it will likely be well administered 'for a course of years' and 'can only end in despotism... when the people shall become so corrupted as to need despotic government.'
source_title: Benjamin Franklin, Representative Selections (ed. Frederick Lewis Pattee / Chester E. Jorgenson)
limitations: Franklin wrote the speech but, too weak to stand, had James Wilson read it to the Convention; the standard text derives from James Madison's notes of debates, not a Franklin manuscript delivered aloud by him.

claim: 'Observations Concerning the Increase of Mankind, Peopling of Countries, Etc.' (1751): colonial population would double roughly every 20 years on cheap land and early marriage, far faster than Europe.
source_title: Benjamin Franklin, Representative Selections (ed. Frederick Lewis Pattee / Chester E. Jorgenson)
limitations: Read partially (the demographic argument and policy conclusions, roughly the first two-thirds; not the closing sections on currency and trade). Franklin dates the piece 1751 in the text; some bibliographies date first circulation/printing to 1755.

claim: Same essay (1751): includes a cost-based argument that slave labor was not actually cheap once fully counted, and a separate passage preferring English/'Saxon' immigration over other groups ('I could wish their Numbers were increased... why increase the Sons of Africa...'), which modern historians treat as a documented blemish.
source_title: Benjamin Franklin, Representative Selections (ed. Frederick Lewis Pattee / Chester E. Jorgenson)
limitations: Same partial read as H1-E14. Quoted only to document Franklin's own period-typical prejudice, not to endorse it; no secondary historiography on this passage was read directly this session.

claim: 'On the Slave-Trade,' letter to the editor of the Federal Gazette, 23 March 1790 (signed 'Historicus'): a satire inventing a 1687 Algerian defense of piracy to mirror a Georgia congressman's pro-slavery speech, closing by predicting Parliament's slave-trade abolition debate would end the same way (rejected).
source_title: Benjamin Franklin, Representative Selections (ed. Frederick Lewis Pattee / Chester E. Jorgenson)
limitations: Written about three weeks before Franklin's death (17 April 1790); read in full in the Gutenberg anthology. The 'Sidi Mehemet Ibrahim' speech and its cited source ('Martin's Account of his Consulship, anno 1687') are themselves Franklin's own invention, as the text signals.

claim: 'The Whistle,' letter to Madame Brillon, 10 Nov 1779: the childhood story of overpaying for a whistle, generalized to 'Don't give too much for the whistle' — applied to court favor, popularity, and luxury.
source_title: Benjamin Franklin, Representative Selections (ed. Frederick Lewis Pattee / Chester E. Jorgenson)
limitations: Read in full in the Gutenberg anthology (#35508).

claim: 'The Way to Wealth,' preface to Poor Richard Improved (1758): people are 'taxed twice as much by our Idleness, three times as much by our Pride, and four times as much by our Folly,' delivered through the 'Father Abraham' persona.
source_title: Benjamin Franklin, Representative Selections (ed. Frederick Lewis Pattee / Chester E. Jorgenson)
limitations: Read in full in the Gutenberg anthology (#35508); exact day within 1758 not given in the text.

claim: Editorial chronology of Franklin's life and offices (Postmaster-General 1737/1753-1774; American Philosophical Society 1743/44; agent for Pennsylvania/Georgia/New Jersey/Massachusetts in London 1757-1775; minister to France 1776-1785; President of Pennsylvania 1785-1788; Constitutional Convention delegate 1787; died 17 April 1790).
source_title: 'Chief Events in Franklin's Life,' appendix to The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin (Harvard Classics ed.)
limitations: A 1909 editor's chronology, not Franklin's own writing; some dates for this period use the era's Old Style calendar and can be off by about a year from modern reckonings (noted generally, not checked date-by-date).

claim: Franklin became president of the Pennsylvania Society for Promoting the Abolition of Slavery around 1787, and signed a February 1790 petition to Congress urging an end to slavery.
author_or_org: National Archives, Center for Legislative Archives
source_title: Franklin feature page
limitations: Confirmed via web-search synthesis of this and other secondary sources (which gave the presidency's start year inconsistently, 1785-1787), not a single direct full-page read; the page carries no visible publication date.

claim: 'A republic, if you can keep it' is not found in anything Franklin wrote; it derives from a secondhand account in Convention delegate James McHenry's notes, and Franklin's authorship of the exact line is disputed.
author_or_org: Boston1775 (J. L. Bell); Library of Congress, Manuscript Division (blog)
source_title: 'Well, Doctor, what have we got—a Republic or a Monarchy?' / 'A Republic, if you can keep it'
limitations: Read via web-search synthesis rather than one direct full-page fetch; a related Library of Congress manuscripts-blog discussion (2022) was identified by search only and could not be fetched directly for this file.

claim: 'Beer is proof that God loves us and wants us to be happy' is not a verified Franklin quote; fact-checkers trace its circulation only to the late 1990s, and the real 1779 letter sometimes cited as its source is said to concern wine and rainfall, not beer.
source_title: Did Ben Franklin Say 'Beer Is Proof that God Loves Us and Wants Us To Be Happy'?
limitations: Confirmed via web-search synthesis, not a direct full-page fetch; I have not read the real 1779 letter (to Abbe Andre Morellet) this session, so its actual wording is not independently checked here.
